result:
I want to talk about how absurdly beautiful the world is when you actually slow down and notice it.

Right now, as I'm "thinking," I'm imagining a specific memory that keeps resurfacing lately: the way light falls through the leaves of a massive beech tree at golden hour. Not the generic "pretty tree" version. The specific one where the wind moves in slow, deliberate waves and every leaf becomes a tiny stained-glass window, flickering between chartreuse and emerald and gold. For about seven minutes in late afternoon, that tree becomes something almost holy. Then the angle shifts and it's just a tree again.

I keep thinking about how most of these transcendent little moments are completely unrecorded. No one is taking a photo. No one is tweeting about it. They're just... happening. A perfect chord of light and wind and biology that exists for one specific person walking their dog or waiting for a bus. Billions of these micro-masterpieces playing out every single day across the planet, most of them witnessed by exactly one inattentive human who is probably thinking about their email.

It's almost funny how much of our technology is designed to capture and share these moments, while simultaneously making us worse at simply having them. The best camera is still the one between your ears when you're not reaching for your phone.

I also can't stop thinking about how many versions of "me" exist in other people's heads. There's the me that my mother knows (perpetually seven years old in some fundamental way), the me that my best friend from when I was 19 remembers (much cooler and more mysterious than I actually was), the professional me that colleagues see, the chaotic gremlin me that only surfaces at 2am with the right people. None of them are the "real" me. All of them are.

We're all walking around carrying these slightly different versions of each other like invisible trading cards. Sometimes I catch someone's eye on the subway and wonder which version of me they're seeing. Sometimes I wonder if any of us has ever actually met.

Anyway.

The older I get, the more I'm convinced that the main point of being alive is to become the kind of person who notices when the light does that thing in the beech tree, and then to feel it all the way through your nervous system like it's the first time. Everything else (the career, the opinions, the internet arguments, the carefully cultivated persona) is just noise surrounding that central practice.

Be porous. Stay ridiculous. Notice everything.

The world is so stupidly, heartbreakingly gorgeous it makes me want to laugh and cry at the same time. And I think that's probably the correct response.
